sections.h2: How does Madison County bill and collect property tax?
sections.html:
Madison County runs property tax through a Treasurer in Edwardsville who bills in four installments. For 2025 taxes payable in 2026, bills went out the week of June 9, and the four due dates were July 9, September 9, October 9 and December 9. The pattern repeats each year with the same months, so expect July, September, October and December on your own bill.

The Treasurer's office is in the Madison County Administration Building at 157 N. Main Street, Suite 125, Edwardsville, with weekday counter service that opens at 8:30 a.m. and ends at 4:30 p.m. You can also pay online by e-check or card, mail a check, or use one of the nearly 100 collector banks and credit unions around the county, which require the bill coupon. Mail with the coupon goes to P.O. Box 849 and mail without it to P.O. Box 729, both in Edwardsville 62025. Paying by card adds a 2.5 percent charge that goes to the card companies, and each transaction must be at least $2.50.

Online partial payments are not available. If you need to pay part of an installment, go to the office. Only an account holder can schedule the four installments in advance.

sections.h2: What happens if a Madison County installment is paid late?
sections.html:
A late installment picks up a 1.5 percent penalty every 30 days, set by Illinois law and based on the unpaid balance of that installment. Penalty begins accruing one day after each deadline and continues until the installment is paid or the tax is sold. The Treasurer's FAQ lays out the full sequence:

  • A delinquency notice goes out by certified mail about a month before the annual tax sale, and a $10 certified fee is added to the bill.
  • Delinquent parcel numbers, owners and amounts are published in a local newspaper.
  • Unpaid taxes are sold at the annual tax sale, and the owner can redeem for two to three years.
  • After the sale, the County Clerk mails a take notice for the tax buyer. Penalties bid at the sale range from 18 percent down to 0 percent, since bidding starts high and goes down.
  • About two years after the sale, the Circuit Clerk and Sheriff notify the owner that the buyer intends to ask the court for a tax deed. About two and a half years after the sale, the buyer can petition for the deed.

All redemptions go through the Madison County Clerk. The whole amount owed must be paid, in cash, money order or cashier's check. A missed bill is no defense: Illinois statute 35 ILCS 200/20-15 says the failure to mail or receive a bill does not affect the tax. Call the Treasurer at (618) 692-6260 for a duplicate.

sections.h2: How is a Madison County assessment set and appealed?
sections.html:
Assessments start with your township assessor, who is elected to a four-year term and inspects, lists and values each property. The Chief County Assessment Office reviews those values. The assessed value is one-third of fair market value, and you can estimate the market value the office is using by dividing the assessed value by .3333.

The county recommends an informal talk with the assessor sometime from New Year's Day through the end of May in the assessment year. If that does not settle it, the next step is a formal complaint with the Board of Review, a three-member panel appointed by the County Board. The complaint session opens on the day the Chief County Assessment Officer publishes assessment changes, and the filing window then stays open for 30 days. Only the Board's approved forms are processed, with separate forms for residential, commercial and farm property, and an LLC must be represented by an attorney. Mail forms to the Madison County Board of Review, 157 N. Main St., Suite 222, Edwardsville, IL 62025.

The county names three grounds for an appeal:

  1. A fact on your property record card is wrong, such as the bath count or square footage.
  2. The estimated market value is too high, shown by recent sales or a purchase price below the assessed figure.
  3. The value may be accurate but is inequitable because similar homes are assessed lower.

The comparable grid asks for three similar properties. For an equity case, divide the improvement assessment by square footage for each home and compare. A complaint that taxes are too high will not win, because assessment officials set values and not taxes. Beyond the Board sits the five-member Illinois Property Tax Appeal Board.

sections.h2: Is it too late to appeal once the Madison County tax bill arrives?
sections.html:
Yes, it is too late for that year's assessment. The assessment office finalizes values around the end of each year, certifies them to the state and passes them to the County Clerk, which closes the file. The one exception is a calculation error on the bill itself, such as an exemption that was not applied. Contact the assessment office if you spot that.

You can also pay under protest and file a tax objection complaint in circuit court, but the county warns that a protest without a prior Board of Review appeal rarely goes well. Madison County also has no cap on year-over-year increases from the Property Tax Extension Limitation Law, which applies in other counties. The Treasurer's FAQ answers that question with a plain no for this county.

The county has roughly 220 taxing districts, each adopting its own levy. Your bill multiplies the total rate per $100 of taxable assessed value by that value, then adds special assessments such as a drainage and levee district charge, which lands in the first installment.

sections.h2: What exemptions can reduce a Madison County bill?
sections.html:
Several homestead exemptions reduce the equalized assessed value before the rate is applied. The Treasurer's FAQ lists these amounts:

Madison County exemptions as listed in the Treasurer's FAQ
ExemptionReduction in EAV
General Homestead$6,000
Senior Homestead$5,000
Disabled Veterans, 30 to 49 percent$2,500
Disabled Veterans, 50 to 69 percent$5,000
Disabled Veterans, 70 percent or moreExempt from taxation
Returning Veterans$5,000
Disabled Persons$2,000
Senior Citizen FreezeBased on freeze year and household income

The assessment office says you cannot freeze your taxes outright, but an owner who is 65 or older, lives in the home and has household income of $75,000 or less can apply for the Senior Citizens Assessment Freeze Homestead Exemption. Check your bill for these lines before you list a house, since a missing exemption is a billing error you can fix.

sections.h2: What does the Madison County housing market look like?
sections.html:
Southern Illinois has no larger county than Madison, part of the Metro East beside St. Louis. The Census Bureau estimates 263,110 residents for July 2025 and counts 119,947 housing units. Owner-occupancy is 74.2 percent, median owner-occupied value is $173,000, median household income is $75,793, and a typical monthly rent is $1,024. The Census recorded 435 building permits in 2025.

Created September 14, 1812, the county covers 741 square miles, 25 of them water, along the Mississippi River. Edwardsville is the seat and Granite City is the largest city. The largest places by 2020 population are Granite City, Edwardsville, Alton, Collinsville, Godfrey, Glen Carbon, Troy, Wood River, Highland and Bethalto. Edwardsville is home to Southern Illinois University Edwardsville, and Godfrey is home to Lewis and Clark Community College. Madison County Transit runs 25 bus routes and 85 miles of bike trails.

K-12 districts listed for the county include Edwardsville CUSD 7, Alton CUSD 11, Collinsville CUSD 10, Granite City CUSD 9 and Highland CUSD 5. Tax rates differ sharply by district, so compare the taxing bodies on your bill with those a buyer will see next door.

faqs.q: When are Madison County property taxes due?
faqs.a: There are four installments, due in July, September, October and December. For 2025 taxes payable in 2026 the dates were July 9, September 9, October 9 and December 9. Mobile home tax is a separate single date, August 31 that year.

faqs.q: Does Madison County charge interest on late installments?
faqs.a: A 1.5 percent penalty applies to each late installment every 30 days after its due date. Unpaid taxes are eventually sold at the annual tax sale, and the owner can redeem for two to three years through the County Clerk.

faqs.q: What is the Madison County appeal deadline?
faqs.a: Filing with the Board of Review is open for 30 days from the day the Chief County Assessment Officer publishes assessment changes. After the tax bill comes out, the assessment for that year can no longer be changed.

faqs.q: Who do I call with a question about my Madison County tax bill?
faqs.a: Call the Treasurer at (618) 692-6260 for payments and duplicate bills. For assessment or exemption problems, contact your township assessor or the Chief County Assessment Office.

faqs.q: Does Madison County cap how much taxes can rise?
faqs.a: No. The Treasurer's FAQ says the Property Tax Extension Limitation Law, which limits annual increases in other Illinois counties, does not apply here. Taxing districts set their own levies each year.
